automation_evidence.finding: Generative-AI conversational assistant raised issues resolved per hour by 14% on average across 5,179 customer-support agents, with a 34% gain for novice/low-skilled agents and minimal effect for experienced ones; also improved customer sentiment and employee retention. Closest large-scale measured analogue to inbound booking/dispatch work in a contractor's office.

Preprint (arXiv, not peer-reviewed): optimization/scenario tool for technician routing and scheduling (skills, time windows, travel costs) reduced travel time by about 16% on a real-life field-service instance from a telecom company; evaluation is on one company's data, not residential HVAC/plumbing.

Preprint (arXiv, 2017, not peer-reviewed): dissimilarity-based machine learning forecast faults on a cohort of 17 HVAC systems using one year of operating data from an Italian hospital, reaching AUC up to 0.96 for certain fault types - evidence for remote diagnostics/predictive maintenance, but a small cohort and non-residential equipment.

Preprint (arXiv, Oct 2025): agent-driven automated building-code review framework combining BIM extraction, retrieval-augmented generation and tool calls to the DOE COMcheck engine; case demonstrations validated lighting allowances under ASHRAE 90.1-2022, and deterministic tool-call pipelines outperformed pure retrieval reasoning. Reports no time-saved or error-rate numbers.

Preprint (arXiv, Jun 2025): LLM-driven semi-automated code compliance checking inside Revit; case studies on a single-family residence and an office building reportedly cut the time and effort of compliance checks and improved accuracy, but results are qualitative with no measured baseline.

Preprint (arXiv, 2024): AI-enhanced IVR for a real call center (speech-to-text, LLM query classification, speech synthesis, Kazakh language) reports reduced operator workload and faster query processing, but publishes no quantified deflection, handle-time or cost figures.

Vendor marketing only: the leading field-service platform's homepage promises higher net profit, better margins, faster cash flow and improved workforce productivity, but publishes no auditable before/after metrics, sample sizes or methodology on that page. Treat all such vendor ROI claims as unverified.

Government demand baseline for the automation business case: BLS projects about 40,600 HVAC mechanic/installer openings per year (2025-35, +11%), 72,700 electrician openings (+9%), 42,000 plumber/pipefitter openings (+7%) and 12,000 roofer openings (+5%), with much of the demand driven by replacement of workers who leave or retire - i.e., the labor these tools would need to substitute for or stretch.

constraints: Refrigerant handling is federally regulated: EPA Clean Air Act Section 608 prohibits knowingly venting ozone-depleting refrigerants and their HFC substitutes while servicing or disposing of AC/refrigeration equipment, requires technician certification and imposes recordkeeping/reporting duties. Any AI-generated work order, refrigerant log or compliance record must be designed around these rules; mis-generated entries create legal exposure.

Licensing and registration: New Jersey regulates electricians, master plumbers and HVACR contractors through state boards, and requires home improvement contractor registration for most residential work (N.J.S.A. 56:8-136 et seq.). Source pages were blocked during this run, so verification of the specific registration thresholds and license scopes is still required before citing them to a client.

Permits and inspection: local construction officials and AHJs govern permits, inspections and code compliance (New Jersey Uniform Construction Code), so AI-drafted scope, code interpretations or compliance checks carry liability if wrong; human sign-off by a licensed contractor is the practical control.

Customer and payment data: home-service firms hold names, home addresses, access instructions, payment card data and call recordings - PCI DSS obligations, call-recording consent rules and general privacy expectations favor private/on-prem or tightly scoped vendor AI rather than consumer chatbots ingesting job details.

Safety and warranty documentation: job records feed OSHA-style safety compliance, manufacturer warranties and insurance claims, so AI-authored notes and estimates must be auditable, editable and attributable to a technician.
trends: Sustained technician scarcity: BLS expects HVAC employment to grow 11% (2025-35), electricians 9%, plumbers 7% and roofers 5%, with roughly 40,600 / 72,700 / 42,000 / 12,000 openings per year respectively and much of the churn from retirement and transfers - replacement demand, not just growth.

New Jersey pays well above the national medians for these trades (2025): HVAC $74,450 in NJ vs $61,010 nationally; plumbers $78,240 vs $63,800; electricians $77,250 vs $63,190; roofers $76,600 vs $55,440. Inference: because each billable technician-hour is expensive and scarce here, throughput gains (more jobs per tech per day, fewer wasted trips) are worth more per point of improvement than in cheaper labor markets.
HVAC is the fastest-growing of the four trades (11% vs 5-9%), consistent with rising cooling demand and heating electrification - inference from BLS projections, not a stated BLS cause.

Seasonality and emergency work shape staffing: BLS notes roofers often work overtime to finish jobs in busy summer months, and plumbers are commonly on call evenings and weekends for emergencies. Inference: demand spikes make answering/booking capacity and after-hours coverage the pinch points AI telephony and scheduling target first.

Margin pressure from small-firm structure: most contractors are owner-operated small businesses where the owner is also the estimator and dispatcher - inference from the O*NET task mix (estimating, ordering, recordkeeping bundled into technician and supervisor roles) rather than from a measured source.

Buyer expectations have shifted toward instant response on web/mobile leads; no verifiable 2025-26 quantified NJ benchmark for lead-response time was located in this run, so treat this as qualitative.
caveats: Evidence for AI outcomes specifically in HVAC/plumbing/electrical/roofing contracting is thin: no randomized or peer-reviewed field study of contractor AI deployments was located in this run. The strongest measured evidence (QJE 2025 / NBER w31161, 5,179 agents, +14% issues per hour) is from customer-support work, which is analogous to a contractor's booking/dispatch desk but not the same setting; transferring that number to a 5-15 person HVAC shop is an inference, not a measured result. Several other items are arXiv preprints that are not peer-reviewed (flagged in the finding text) and report small samples or qualitative results. The BLS OOH projection figures are solid but describe labor demand, not automation outcomes. Wage figures come from the BLS Public Data API (OEWS May 2025 series, e.g. OEUS340000000000049902113 = New Jersey statewide, occupation 49-9021, annual median), not from a rendered table page; the metro figure uses OEWS area code 0035620, which I take to be the New York-Newark-Jersey City MSA that contains Middlesex County - that code-to-area mapping is an inference from the CBSA code, and BLS publishes no separate Edison/New Brunswick estimate. Wage medians blend residential service and commercial/industrial work. The tools list combines one vendor site verified in this run (ServiceTitan) with widely known products that were not individually verified, so product names should be confirmed before they appear in client-facing material. All web search providers were rate-limited or unavailable during this run, so discovery relied on O*NET, BLS, arXiv/Crossref APIs and direct page fetches; relevant peer-reviewed field-service studies may exist that were not found.
data_gaps: No New Jersey- or Middlesex County-specific study measuring time saved, error reduction or revenue recovered from AI in home-service contracting was found.

No separate BLS OEWS estimate exists for an 'Edison-New Brunswick' area in the May 2025 release that could be opened in this run; Middlesex County is covered by the New York-Newark-Jersey City metro figure reported here (area-code mapping inferred).

New Jersey Division of Consumer Affairs pages (home improvement contractor registration, electrical/plumbing/HVACR licensing) were blocked by bot protection, so state registration and licensing requirements could not be primary-sourced - verify before quoting them.
Adoption rate of AI tools among NJ contractors (and AI use by firm size in construction trades) could not be sourced; Census BTOS AI supplements are JavaScript-rendered and were not retrievable.

No peer-reviewed field experiment on AI answering/dispatch in residential service contracting (deflection rate, booked-job rate, average ticket, no-show rate) surfaced; vendor case studies report such numbers but were not citable at acceptable strength.
Roofing-specific AI evidence (drone/aerial damage assessment, estimate accuracy) was searched via arXiv and Crossref but no study with usable measured outcomes was retrieved in this run.

Web search providers were unavailable (rate limits) for most of the session; a follow-up pass with working search should look for trade-press surveys (PHCC, ACCA, NRCA) and any 2025-26 field-service AI outcome studies.
